children: By Nick Timiraos

WASHINGTON-The Federal Reserve raised interest rates Wednesday for the first time in three years, a sharp reversal that began taking back cuts it made last year and implicitly undercut the White House's insistence that inflation isn't a concern.

The increase, approved unanimously, will raise the benchmark federal-funds rate range by a quarter point to between 3.75% and 4%. The vast majority of officials penciled in one more hike this year in interest-rate projections released after their meeting.

Chairman Kevin Warsh vowed shortly after taking office in May to end an overshoot of the Fed's 2% target now in its sixth year and followed through with an increase that had been widely anticipated in recent days.

The rate hike scrambled an account the White House had offered of the man tapped by President Trump for the job in January. Trump and his allies had cast pressure to raise rates as coming from a committee hostile to Warsh, who last year said he would have cut rates sooner than the Fed ultimately did.

It also followed a lost year in the Fed's inflation fight. The central bank has made no progress toward its 2% goal since mid-2025, including after cutting rates three times late last year to guard against a labor-market slowdown. Instead, the Iran war has lifted energy prices, and the AI boom has driven an investment surge that has buoyed the economy and markets.

"Today's policy action will support a timelier return to the committee's 2% goal," the rate-setting committee said in its policy statement. It cited elevated uncertainty due in part from geopolitics and omitted previous language that had attributed elevated inflation partly to supply shocks.
Analysts had said that despite intense focus of late on monthly inflation data, the biggest change to the outlook has come from a run-up in energy and commodity prices.
"It's the fact that the war in Iran has re-intensified and the energy price shock is getting bigger again," said William Dudley, the former New York Fed president.

Diesel prices have climbed toward record highs, worsened by a refining bottleneck that Ukrainian strikes on Russian energy infrastructure have deepened. Crude around $100 a barrel understates what businesses are actually paying: Diesel is behaving as though oil were at $200, said Dudley. Costs are working into shipping and airfares, and the effects look likely to last longer than officials expected.

As energy prices have climbed, so have long-term Treasury yields, which recently reached their highest levels in nearly two decades, with the 10-year note recently trading above 5%. Investors have attributed the rise to a mix of forces: higher expected growth from the AI build-out, competition for capital from data-center borrowing, and questions over how high the Fed will have to raise rates to get inflation down.

The Fed's benchmark rate most directly affects short-term borrowing such as credit cards and new loans for autos, which reprice quickly. The costs that matter most to many households and businesses, including mortgage rates, track longer-term Treasury yields-and those have risen as investors expect future rate increases.

The 30-year mortgage rate climbed to nearly 7% last week, the highest in nearly a year, according to a survey by the Mortgage Bankers Association released Wednesday. It stood at 6% in February, before the U.S. bombing campaign began.

The decision leaves open what exactly will follow. The Fed rarely makes just one adjustment after it concludes a turn toward raising or lowering rates is warranted, because a quarter-point higher or lower doesn't do much on its own to change borrowing conditions.

In new projections, 16 out of 18 meeting participants penciled in at least one more increase this year, which would take rates to just above 4%. Only four penciled in rates ending next year below that level.
What has changed
A Fed raising short-term rates into a bond market already pricing higher inflation reflects how far the fight has moved from where officials expected it to be.

Officials ended a sprint to lift rates to a two-decade high in 2023. They began cutting in 2024 as price growth slowed, paused early last year as tariffs threatened to push inflation back up, then resumed reductions last fall.

Last year's cuts were insurance against a labor-market slump that never arrived. The unemployment rate has drifted down to 4.1% after rising to 4.5% late last year, and hiring has exceeded the pace needed to absorb new workers.

Because inflation stayed higher than officials expected, the inflation-adjusted or "real" policy rate is lower now than when they cut. "Having inflation high and real interest rates very low for a sustained period seems like a bad idea," said William English, a former senior Fed official now at Yale.

The textbook response to a supply shock is to look through it on the theory that it passes before higher rates take effect. The Fed has faced at least two such shocks over the past two years, from tariffs and higher energy prices from the Iran war. The AI build-out, meanwhile, is adding demand faster than supply can meet it.

The case for waiting rests on recent data. Economists at Goldman Sachs say the economic case for raising rates is weak. Underlying price growth over the last three months is lower than the three months before that, and much of the overshoot traces to one-off factors rather than an overheating economy.

The counterargument is that the case for waiting depends on assumptions that aren't holding up. Energy prices were expected to have receded by now. A softening job market was supposed to take pressure off wages and prices. Instead, hiring has steadied and some economists think more employers will soon have to compete harder for workers, which could stoke new cost pressures. Officials who want to move say the question isn't what the last three months showed, but what would give confidence that price growth will be muted six months from now.

Rate increases won't produce more crude oil or slow an AI build-out that is largely insensitive to borrowing costs, since the capital is committed and expected returns dwarf what a quarter point changes. What they can do is cool the rest of the economy enough to ease the strain on supply.
A learning curve

Warsh raised rates at his third meeting as chairman after having suggested one year ago that the Fed was too slow to cut. At his first press conference in June, Warsh cast the Fed's inflation record as a credibility problem that he would fix.

But he said little at his first two meetings about how he read the economy or what would move him. Warsh has argued for years that narrating the Fed's outlook ties its hands. Investors were left to infer his views, and the guesses ranged from a chairman who would delay hikes as long as possible to one who was ready to raise rates.

At the July press conference, long-term Treasury yields rose while Warsh spoke, and they never came back down. Investors were demanding more compensation to hold long-term debt. The move was "essentially a vote on monetary policy credibility, one that was not recovered," said James Egelhof, chief U.S. economist at BNP Paribas.

Warsh's colleagues, meanwhile, were growing more uneasy holding rates steady. While the vote to hold steady in June was unanimous, three officials dissented in July for an increase. Minutes of the meeting later showed others ready to join if inflation didn't improve.

Analysts read Warsh's keynote speech last month as an effort to repair any damage. In his talk, Warsh said he saw little evidence that borrowing conditions were restraining the economy, and that the summer's better inflation readings hadn't convinced him the underlying trend was improving. Odds of a September rate increase rose and kept climbing as economic developments suggested sturdier growth and stickier inflation.
"That by itself then creates a bit of pressure to follow up with actions rather than just have it be words," Dudley said. Warsh "sort of backed himself a little bit into a corner."
